source: Belfield, S. and Brown, C. (2010). Guidebook on Upland Crops in Cambodia: Corn (សៀវភៅណែនាំ ស្តីពីដំណាំតំបន់ខ្ពង់រាបនៅក្នុងប្រទេសកម្ពុជា៖ ដំណាំពោត). ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
Corn (Zea mays), known in Khmer as ពោត, has been cultivated by humans for roughly 7,000-9,000 years and is grown across a wide range of climates and management systems worldwide. In Cambodia, corn is grown under diverse agro-ecological conditions using both traditional and improved methods, and it is one of the country's most important upland (non-rice) crops.

Two broad market types are grown in Cambodia. White/glutinous corn (ពោតស, sometimes called waxy corn) is grown mainly for direct human consumption -- it is commonly boiled and sold fresh, and tends to fetch a higher price than field corn. Yellow/dent corn (ពោតលឿង) is grown mainly as a commercial/feed crop and dominates the export-oriented value chain, especially in Battambang and Pailin provinces.

A national demonstration trial run jointly by CARDI and ACIAR (project ASEM/2000/109, comparing farmer practice against improved practice components on the CP888 hybrid, Early Wet Season 2006) illustrates the size of the yield gap in Cambodia: farmer-practice yield averaged around 4.2-5.0 t/ha, while combining improved practices (soil management, fertilizer, weed control, plant density) lifted yield to roughly 5.6-5.9 t/ha in the trial. This gap between farmers' typical yields and the crop's potential yield (cited elsewhere in the source as high as 10-15 t/ha under research conditions) is presented as the central rationale for the practices covered in this guide.
